analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workplace anti-harassment law, bans forced arbitration of discrimination claims, and phases out the subminimum tipped wage.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2024 with 22 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents, the bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tighten federal workplace civil rights law. Employers with even one employee would have to adopt anti-harassment policies and training; harassment would be judged on the totality of circumstances, with a single incident enough in some cases; damages caps would come off; deadlines to sue would lengthen; and independent contractors, interns, and volunteers would gain protection. It would also ban forced arbitration of discrimination claims, restrict nondisclosure agreements, and raise the tipped minimum wage from $2.13 to $3.60, then by $1.50 a year until it equals the regular federal minimum wage.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face harassment or discrimination — especially women, LGBTQ workers, low-income and tipped workers, and contractors and interns who currently fall outside federal employment law. Workers with discrimination claims would regain access to court instead of being pushed into forced arbitration, and tipped workers would move toward a full minimum wage their employers must pay directly.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every employer with 15 or more employees to maintain a comprehensive anti-harassment policy with multiple reporting channels, confidentiality protections, and anti-retaliation rules, with fines of up to $1,000 per violation ($5,000 for repeat or willful violations) [S2].

Writes a harassment standard into statute: conduct is judged on the totality of circumstances, incidents are considered in the aggregate, and a single incident can qualify — overturning narrow court readings of 'severe or pervasive' [S2].

Removes the caps on compensatory and punitive damages in employment discrimination cases and extends the statutes of limitations, so victims have more time to sue and can recover more when they win [S2].
Prohibits mandatory arbitration of discrimination claims and limits the use of nondisclosure agreements, restoring workers' ability to take claims to court and speak about them publicly [S2].
Extends protections to independent contractors, interns, fellows, volunteers, and trainees, and covers employers with as few as one employee (currently 15) [S2].

Phases out the separate tipped minimum wage: $3.60 an hour in year one, rising $1.50 a year until it equals the regular federal minimum wage, with employees guaranteed the right to keep their tips [S2].

Clarifies that discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, and pregnancy is unlawful sex discrimination, and bars using the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense to Title VII claims [S2].

Creates a national prevalence survey on workplace harassment, funds civil legal assistance grants for low-income workers, and establishes a state advocacy system, so more workers can actually get a lawyer [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the direct costs: compliance with mandatory policies and training, exposure to uncapped damages and longer filing windows, loss of forced arbitration as a cheaper dispute channel, and — for restaurants and other tipped employers — the gradual elimination of the tip credit that lets them count customer tips toward the minimum wage. Small businesses newly covered down to one employee face these rules for the first time, though the bill provides free model policies and training materials for them.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on businesses of every size: coverage drops from 15 employees to 1, and employers must adopt policies, run training, and post materials, with federal fines for noncompliance [S2].

Removing damages caps and extending filing deadlines increases litigation exposure and settlement pressure on employers across the economy, costs that can translate into higher prices or more defensive HR practices [S2].

The single-incident and totality-of-circumstances standard makes it materially easier to bring — and harder to dismiss — harassment claims, which supporters intend but employers and courts would have to absorb [S2].

Eliminating the tipped minimum wage raises labor costs for restaurants and bars, an industry with thin margins; opponents of tip-credit repeal have long argued it can lead to reduced hours or pressure on tipping, though the bill guarantees employees keep their tips [S2].
The bill bars a religious-freedom defense to Title VII claims, which religious employers and institutions would view as a serious constraint on their operations [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the upside is substantial: a realistic path to challenge harassment, a lawyer if they are low-income, the end of forced arbitration in these cases, and a guaranteed full minimum wage for tipped workers. The costs are real but ordinary costs of enforcing civil rights: compliance paperwork for employers, higher litigation exposure, and higher labor costs in tipped industries. The design softens the burden on small employers with free model materials, but dropping coverage to one employee and removing damages caps without any size accommodation is aggressive, and opponents would fairly argue it shifts significant cost to small businesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced the BE HEARD in the Workplace Act on July 31, 2024, joined by 22 cosponsors including Sens. Hirono, Brown, Baldwin, Booker, Sanders, Warren, and Wyden [S1][S2][S3].
All 22 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Republican signed on [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction — its only action [S4].
The HELP Committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].
This was the bill's latest iteration; versions of the BE HEARD Act had been introduced in prior Congresses without advancing to law, a pattern widely reported.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off: the mandatory anti-harassment programs, uncapped damages, forced-arbitration ban, and phase-out of the $2.13 tipped minimum wage never took effect. Restaurant and bar owners keeping the tip credit gained the most.

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.role: U.S. Senator from Washington; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 22 cosponsors

for.name: 22 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill unified Democratic support but no Republican partner

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (Chair Bernie Sanders)
against.role: Committee of referral; controls whether the bill gets a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died at referral with no further action in the committee's record

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; it never received a vote in either chamber

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Provided zero cosponsors, leaving the bill with no apparent path to 60 votes even if it had reached the floor

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and no Republican supported the bill; it never advanced far enough to produce a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill phases out the $2.13 tipped minimum wage, requiring these employers to eventually pay the full federal minimum wage directly while workers keep their tips. The industry's interest in keeping the tip credit runs directly against the wage gains for the roughly millions of tipped workers.

industries.industry: Employers using forced arbitration and NDAs
industries.note: The bill bans mandatory arbitration of discrimination claims and restricts nondisclosure agreements, removing two tools employers use to keep harassment disputes private and out of court. Workers regain the courtroom access those tools took away.

industries.industry: Broad employer community, especially small businesses
industries.note: Coverage drops to employers with even one employee, and all covered employers must adopt policies, run training, and face uncapped damages and longer filing windows. Small employers get free model materials from the EEOC, which offsets some but not all of the new burden.

industries.industry: HR compliance and anti-harassment training providers
industries.note: Mandatory policies and research-based training requirements would create new demand for compliance services and training programs. Their gain rides on the same provisions that protect workers.

industries.industry: Employment plaintiffs' bar and civil legal aid
industries.note: Grants for legal assistance to low-income workers, longer statutes of limitations, and uncapped damages would expand the market for employment discrimination representation and fund legal aid directly.
